records.title: Towards Adaptive Social Protection Systems in Latin America and the Caribbean : A Synthesis Note on Using Social Protection to Mitigate and Respond to Disaster Risk
records.abstract: This synthesis note is the first in a series of guidance notes which aim to serve as a consultation tool in the design of Adaptive Social Protection (ASP) Systems in Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries to better address disasters and climate risks. While these notes focus on disasters caused by natural hazards, the framework and lessons are also applicable to other types of emergencies and shocks, including economic shocks, health pandemics, and shocks caused by conflict. The note provides a stocktaking of the specific disaster risks faced by LAC countries provides an overview of SP systems and performance in LAC countries, establishes a general framework to assess ASP capacity in LAC, and provides guidance on better using SP systems in LAC to support Disaster Risk Management (DRM) pillars.

records.abstract: This note provides guidance on how to carry out a 'drill-down' examination of domestic resource mobilization (DRM) for increased health sector fiscal space to ensure progress towards universal health coverage (UHC). The guidance note specifically aims to identify a given country’s most critical opportunities (and constraints) to increase domestically-resourced public financing for universal health coverage (UHC) so that policy-makers can make informed decisions to tackle primary challenges.

records.title: Social Protection Systems for Refugees in the Great Lakes Region
records.abstract: Refugee inclusion in national social protection systems in fragile and conflict affected settings is central to development responses to protracted displacement. Focusing on the Great Lakes Region (GLR) - Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, and Uganda - this report assesses the capacity of existing social protection systems to support refugees beyond short term humanitarian assistance and contribute to resilience, self reliance, and social cohesion. Using an adapted adaptive social protection framework, the analysis examines five core system dimensions:(a) policies and legal rights, (b) institutional arrangements, (c) programs and delivery systems, (d) data and information systems, and (e) financing. The report draws on policy and legal analysis, administrative and expenditure data, and country level program evidence to map current practices and identify binding constraints to refugee inclusion. Findings show that while GLR countries have ratified international refugee frameworks and demonstrate growing policy openness to development oriented approaches, refugee assistance remains predominantly humanitarian, externally financed, and weakly integrated into national systems. Government led social safety net programs—including cash transfers, and labor intensive public works—have begun to include refugees in selected contexts, but coverage remains limited and uneven. records.title: From Short-Term Aid to Long-Term Solutions : Social Protection as a Pathway for Refugee Inclusion in the Great Lakes Region - Discussion Note
records.abstract: This note emphasizes the urgent need for development strategies beyond short-term aid to address protracted refugee crises in the Great Lakes Region (GLR). Due to major cuts to international aid, the paper advocates for integrating refugees into national social protection systems to enhance resilience, social inclusion, and socioeconomic development, reducing tensions with host communities. In fact, this note proposes a pragmatic pathway for progressive inclusion of refugees into national social protection systems, complementing not substituting humanitarian action in protracted settings. Transitioning to development programs requires legal and policy reforms, alignment with national systems, flexible financing, and regional cooperation. Challenges include increasing refugee vulnerability in regions with weak social protection systems and funding. The note proposes a layered financing model that couples domestic effort with predictable, multi-year concessional resources, disaster-risk financing and contingency mechanisms, and budget tagging to track refugee-related expenditure within government systems. Greater dialogue among governments, regional bodies, and development partners is essential to include refugees in national development plans and adapt social protection systems, considering regional approaches where appropriate. records.title: Coverage or Intensity of Support ? Adaptive Social Protection to Reduce Disaster-Related Poverty
records.abstract: Disasters due to natural hazards pose a significant threat to people’s well-being and increase the risk of poverty, particularly in vulnerable populations. This paper provides a novel global estimate of poverty due to disasters, showing that 25.6 million people are at risk of poverty due to disasters, 12.7 million thereof facing extreme poverty. Disaster-related consumption losses amount to $758 billion and cause well-being losses equivalent to a uniform drop in consumption of $1,143 billion. Adaptive social protection aims to mitigate these risks by integrating social protection, disaster risk management, and climate adaptation to enhance disaster resilience. Yet, given limited resources, finding the right balance between coverage (the breadth of the population reached by the measure) and intensity (the extent to which each beneficiary is supported) of policy measures is challenging. The paper systematically analyzes this trade-off for various adaptive social protection measures across 131 countries. Total benefits are usually largest for the scenarios with the most extensive coverage and intensity, but the optimal expansion path differs between measures and by country income groups. records.title: Social Protection Systems for Internally Displaced Populations, Returnees, and Host Communities in the Great Lakes Region
records.abstract: Social protection systems for internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, and host communities in fragile and conflict affected settings are critical to sustainable responses to protracted and cyclical displacement. Focusing on the Great Lakes Region (GLR), Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, and Uganda, this report assesses the capacity of national social protection systems to address the socioeconomic vulnerabilities of displacement affected populations beyond short term humanitarian assistance. Using an adapted adaptive social protection framework, the analysis examines five system dimensions: (a) policies and legal rights, (b) institutional arrangements, (c) programs and delivery systems, (d) data and information systems, and (e) financing. Findings show that despite regional and international commitments, most notably the Kampala Convention, social protection systems remain weakly equipped to respond to large scale internal displacement and return, with assistance largely delivered through humanitarian channels, particularly in conflict affected areas. The report concludes that strengthening government led social protection systems to systematically include IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable host communities on the basis of need is critical to enhancing resilience, supporting reintegration, and reducing long term dependence on humanitarian assistance in the GLR.

records.abstract: This report documents advances and challenges to strengthening low- and middle-income countries' social protection and labor systems. It discusses ways to gradually close the coverage gap to protect the world’s poorest households. records.title: Global Insights on Social Registries : Coverage and Beyond
records.abstract: Social protection and labor programs, such as social assistance, social insurance, or labor and economic inclusion interventions, create pathways to self-reliance, financial inclusion, and financial stability. And when crises hit, they become critical lifelines. Yet, in 2024, nearly 2 billion people still lacked any form of protection and at the current pace, closing the gap would take another two decades. In the context of the polycrisis, including slow economic growth, fiscal pressures, fragility and conflict, food insecurity, escalating climate risks, and the lingering effects of COVID-19, limited social protection coverage is hindering effective responses. Strengthening social protection systems and expanding coverage have therefore never been more urgent. The World Bank, in collaboration with partners, has committed to support an additional 500 million poor and vulnerable individuals with social protection and labor programs by 2030. This ambitious goal demands innovative and efficient approaches to ensure that available resources are directed to those in need, while minimizing administrative burdens and transaction costs. records.title: Scaling up Social Assistance Payments as Part of the Covid19 Pandemic Response
records.abstract: Globally, the expansion of social assistance is among the most common public policy responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. The scale of these programs is unprecedented both in terms of government spending and the share of the population receiving social assistance. The challenge of quickly determining who would be eligible for these transfers highlighted gaps in information about workers in the informal sector and their families and other vulnerable groups. A review of some of these experiences reveals the importance of certain ‘assets’ such as a robust digital identification system and other key registries in areas such as tax and social security. Countries with superior and more inclusive assets in this regard were able to move more quickly than those without them. This may lead governments to expedite the investments required in this infrastructure and better prepare them for future crises. records.title: Built to Include - Reimagining Social Protection in the Middle East and North Africa
records.abstract: COVID-19 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have had – and are continuing to have—a devasting impact on living standards. But most countries in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) were already struggling with poverty and vulnerability before the pandemic. This report argues that labor market exclusion is at the root of the problem. Work opportunities in the region are limited, particularly for women and youth, and most workers are engaged in low-productivity informal jobs. While creating more and better jobs requires a dynamic private sector, this report argues that social protection policies can play a crucial role in reducing labor market exclusion. Such policies can help facilitate access to productive employment, protect workers, and provide a safety net for people who are left behind. However, according to the report, social protection policies in countries across MENA are falling short of that role. For example, most of the poor do not receive income support, and most workers are not covered by pensions or unemployment insurance. records.abstract: Investing in better data systems is critical to maximize the impact of social protection programs as more and more countries around the world are aiming to not only reduce poverty and inequality but also to achieve Universal Social Protection (USP). If not managed well, the expansion of services and beneficiaries can contribute to fragmentation in program processes and systems that will result in higher administrative costs, lack of coordination, and duplication in processes. records.title: Long Term Financial Projections of the VSS Compulsory Pension Scheme
records.abstract: The Vietnamese Social Security Institute (VSS) administers mandatory social insurance benefits for six different contingencies - sickness, maternity, old-age and survivorship (pension), labor accident and occupational disease (LAOD), unemployment insurance and health insurance. The rapid ageing of Vietnam’s population poses a serious challenge to the young compulsory pension system. The pension scheme mandated for those in the formal sector is known as the Retirement and Survivorship Allowance Fund (RSAF). This note presents long term projections using the World Bank’s Pension Reform Options Simulation Toolkit (PROST) model in response to the government’s request and in the context of a planned reform to the Social Insurance Law in 2023. This note is the first step in the process of providing inputs that can help policymakers in the Ministry of Labor, Invalids and Social Affairs (MOLISA) and Vietnamese Social Security (VSS) to determine what parametric changes are needed in order not only to ensure long run sustainability but also to ensure adequacy and fairness across and within generations. records.title: Assessment of Identification for Social Protection in Saint Lucia
records.abstract: With a quarter of the country’s population living below the poverty line, the social protection landscape in Saint Lucia is highly fragmented across both governmental and non-governmental agencies. The lack of interoperable sources of information results in potential errors and missed opportunities to take advantage of valuable data to design and implement evidence-based policies. The different databases managed by institutions do not exchange information on a regular basis and through automated processes, making it difficult to map individuals and households across different social protection programs. This hampers the chance to connect potential beneficiaries with benefits and services provided by the Ministry of Equity, Social Justice, Local Government and Empowerment (MoEQ) and other ministries such as Health, Education and Agriculture. To address these challenges, the Saint Lucia Human Capital Resilience Project (HCRP) is supporting the country in the design and implementation of a Social Information System (SIS). records.title: Botswana Social Protection Programs and Systems Review
records.abstract: Botswana has a long history of important social protection programs, and the World Bank Group is pleased to be part of that continued effort to help improve social protection in the country. This Botswana social protection programs and systems review takes stock of the current performance of Botswana's social protection programs and systems, in particular the social assistance programs, and their appropriateness in the face of the poverty and vulnerability profile of the country. Social protection programs are most effective when they are shaped to match the current social, fiscal, economic and policy landscape of the country. In the context of Botswana, despite improvements, they still face several challenges, especially from the impact of Coronavirus (COVID-19), which has intensified vulnerabilities and has increased the risks of falling into poverty, especially for women and children. More is needed to protect the poor and vulnerable from shocks such as these, especially given the relatively low Human Capital Index, persistently high unemployment, and uneven poverty reduction across the country. records.title: Assessment of VSS’s Voluntary Pension Scheme and Policy Recommendations
records.abstract: Vietnam is a country on the cusp of a dramatic ageing of the population. It has an ambitious goal of expanding contributor coverage to 60 percent of the labor force and beneficiary coverage to 60 percent of people beyond retirement age, by 2030. Realizing these goals will likely be difficult without greater policy innovation and public spending. Without a major shift in pension policy, the contrast between the pension "haves" and "have nots" will become even starker in the coming decades. The high rates of informality, limited beneficiary coverage under social pension and low contributor coverage in the voluntary pension scheme were all known challenges even before the pandemic but the rise in informal employment and decreased probability of social insurance coverage have added to the challenge. The need to expand pension coverage to informal workers and the challenges associated with it, was well documented and understood by policymakers in Vietnam prior to the Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.
